content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed comprehensive guidelines for the prevention and treatment of maternal peripartum infections, which are a significant cause of maternal morbidity and mortality worldwide. These infections, occurring around the time of childbirth, account for approximately 10% of the global burden of maternal deaths. While the majority of these deaths occur in low-income countries, maternal infections remain a critical cause of mortality even in high-income settings. Beyond the immediate risks, women who experience peripartum infections are at increased risk of long-term complications, including chronic pelvic pain, fallopian tube blockage, and secondary infertility. Additionally, maternal infections are associated with an estimated one million neonatal deaths annually. The WHO guidelines emphasize the importance of preventive measures to reduce the risk of maternal peripartum infections, particularly in the presence of known risk factors such as prolonged rupture of membranes, multiple vaginal examinations, manual removal of the placenta, and cesarean sections. Globally, the most common intervention for preventing and managing maternal infections is the use of antibiotics for prophylaxis and treatment. However, inappropriate or excessive use of antibiotics in obstetric care is a widespread issue, contributing to the emergence of antimicrobial resistance. This has significant implications for global health, as resistant bacterial strains undermine efforts to ensure effective treatment options. The WHO's global strategy for containing antimicrobial resistance highlights the need for judicious use of antibiotics at all levels of the healthcare system. This includes ensuring access to appropriate treatments while minimizing the misuse of antimicrobials. The guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations to guide healthcare professionals and policymakers on the appropriate use of antibiotics for preventing and treating maternal peripartum infections. These recommendations align with the WHO's broader strategy to improve maternal and neonatal outcomes. The primary goal of the guidelines is to consolidate effective interventions to reduce the global burden of maternal infections and their complications during childbirth. This effort is part of WHO's commitment to improving the quality of care for leading causes of maternal mortality, particularly those occurring around the time of childbirth. The guidelines present evidence-based recommendations for preventing and treating genital tract infections during labor, childbirth, and the postpartum period, with the aim of improving outcomes for both mothers and newborns. The target audience for these guidelines includes healthcare professionals responsible for developing national and local health protocols and policies, as well as managers of maternal and child health programs and policymakers in all settings. The guidelines are also intended for obstetricians, midwives, nurses, and general practitioners who provide direct care to pregnant women. Additionally, the information in the guidelines can be used to develop job aids and training tools for healthcare workers to enhance their ability to prevent and treat maternal peripartum infections. The development of the guidelines followed standard WHO procedures, as outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. This process included identifying priority questions and critical outcomes, retrieving and synthesizing evidence, formulating recommendations, and planning for dissemination, implementation, and evaluation. The evidence supporting the recommendations was synthesized using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) approach. Systematic reviews were conducted to prepare evidence profiles for prioritized questions, and a technical consultation was convened in April 2015, during which an international group of experts formulated and approved the recommendations. The WHO technical consultation adopted 20 recommendations addressing prioritized questions related to the prevention and treatment of maternal peripartum infections. These recommendations cover a range of interventions, including the use of antimicrobial agents for vaginal and cesarean births, antibiotic prophylaxis for infection-prone conditions and obstetric procedures, and the management of specific infections such as chorioamnionitis and postpartum endometritis. Each recommendation was graded based on the quality of evidence (very low, low, moderate, or high) and the balance of benefits and harms, stakeholder values and preferences, and resource implications. To ensure clarity and practical application, the contributing experts provided additional remarks for each recommendation. Users of the guidelines are encouraged to refer to these remarks and the evidence summaries in the full version of the guidelines for further details. The recommendations will be regularly reviewed and updated as new evidence becomes available, with major updates occurring at least every five years. WHO welcomes suggestions for additional questions to be included in future updates of the guidelines.
